items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Tony took advantage of the seven string and we made a couple of beautiful records together because Tony was a very lyrical player.

ctx.x: When you got together to do a duo record with some of those people, mostly just talking through tunes, picking out tunes, did you rehearse it a lot?

Well at first I would say with Tony Mottola, Tony took advantage of the seven string and we made a couple of beautiful records together because Tony was a very lyrical player. And then the same with George Barnes, and it was a different approach. George and I went through a fake book one night out in Jersey with the machine, the recording machine on, we played one tune after another, like just turned page after page. Go into it, play it, and we had, oh we had enough for about ten albums. But it was the beginning…

items.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015
items.q: So Tony Mottola and I got together and we made up an Italian medley.

ctx.x: The president of Italy. He was a guest. So Tony Mottola and I got together and we made up an Italian medley. And that was big. I have a picture of that, a movie of it.

You know you mention the Italian thing and I thought of you both on Christmas day, because I put on John’s Christmas CD. And I remember when I put it on I was thinking, I wonder what it’s like in the Pizzarelli house today. Do you have big gatherings?

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Everybody was a jazz — I mean mostly all the guitar players, when we started doing those rock & roll dates, every one — Mundell Lowe, Billy Bauer, Chuck Wayne, Tony Mottola, Al Caiola — all great players, playing three chords.

ctx.x: And most of the guys were from the jazz and the swing—

Everybody was. Everybody was a jazz — I mean mostly all the guitar players, when we started doing those rock & roll dates, every one — Mundell Lowe, Billy Bauer, Chuck Wayne, Tony Mottola, Al Caiola — all great players, playing three chords.

That’s cool. How did you handle the business end of it? You know in these days of agents and cell phones and pagers and all that kind of stuff it’s a little different. How did you get the word to report to a certain place, and how did you set your dates.
